# Social Care and Support — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/social-care-and-support-ireland.html

# Social care and support — Ireland

Irish social work and social care pathways are delivered through HSE services, disability and community providers, Tusla and other agencies. Identify the responsible service, the person’s outcomes, eligibility or assessment process, family and carer needs, advocacy and complaints route. Do not import a UK Care Act threshold.

Separate needs assessment, service planning, funding and review. Record communication, cultural identity, consent, disagreement, contingency and who will act. Check current HSE policy and local service arrangements.

[HSE safeguarding and social-care information](https://www2.healthservice.hse.ie/organisation/national-pppgs/safeguarding-vulnerable-persons-at-risk-of-abuse-2014-national-policy-procedures/)

# Decision-Making and Capacity — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/assisted-decision-making-and-capacity-ireland.html

# Decision-making and capacity — Ireland

The Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) Act 2015, as amended and commenced on 26 April 2023, provides a functional, issue- and time-specific framework. It established decision-support arrangements and the Decision Support Service, replacing the former wardship approach over the transition period.

Support the person to decide, identify the least restrictive support arrangement and check the authority of a decision-making assistant, co-decision-maker, decision-making representative, advance healthcare directive or other arrangement. Check current regulations and Decision Support Service guidance.

[Assisted Decision-Making Act](https://www.gov.ie/en/department-of-justice-home-affairs-and-migration/publications/assisted-decision-making-capacity-act-2015/)

---

# Restrictions and Liberty — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/restrictions-and-liberty-ireland.html

# Restrictions and liberty — Ireland

Ireland does not use the England, Wales or Northern Ireland DoLS routes. Examine the lawful basis for any restriction, the Assisted Decision-Making (Capacity) framework, relevant health or residential-care law, constitutional and human-rights protections, consent, objection, necessity and proportionality.

Describe the actual arrangements, support to communicate, review and challenge route. Do not treat a diagnosis, a capacity finding or a provider policy as authority for confinement. Seek current legal and safeguarding advice for the setting.

[Decision Support Service](https://decisionsupportservice.ie/)

# Mental Health — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/mental-health-ireland.html

# Mental health — Ireland

The Mental Health Act 2001 and Mental Health Commission standards and guidance govern approved-centre admission, treatment safeguards, advocacy and tribunal review. Identify the purpose of intervention, the person’s rights, independent advocacy, responsible professionals and review route.

Separate mental-health detention from physical healthcare, decision-support arrangements, restrictions and safeguarding. Check current Mental Health Commission guidance and local HSE procedures; do not import Mental Health Act sections from any UK jurisdiction.

[Mental Health Commission](https://www.mhcirl.ie/)

# Adult Safeguarding — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/safeguarding-adults-ireland.html

# Safeguarding adults — Ireland

Use current HSE safeguarding policy and local safeguarding and protection teams for adults who may experience abuse, exploitation, neglect or harm. Establish the person’s account, immediate safety, communication, consent, decision-support needs, advocacy and desired outcomes.

Information-sharing and referral routes depend on the HSE service and circumstances. Follow the current national policy and local procedure, record the lawful reason for sharing and do not invent a UK statutory threshold.

[HSE safeguarding policy](https://www2.healthservice.hse.ie/organisation/national-pppgs/safeguarding-vulnerable-persons-at-risk-of-abuse-2014-national-policy-procedures/)

# Children, Families and Transitions — Ireland — Ireland

Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/children-and-families-ireland.html

# Children and families — Ireland

Use Children First: National Guidance for the Protection and Welfare of Children 2017, the Children First Act 2015 and Tusla procedures. Mandated persons and relevant-service providers have specific obligations, including reporting and child safeguarding statements.

Listen to the child, explain confidentiality and reporting in an accessible way, record facts separately from analysis and coordinate Tusla, An Garda Síochána, education, health and family support as appropriate.

[Children First guidance and legislation](https://www.tusla.ie/children-first/children-first-guidance-and-legislation/)

# Rights, participation and recording — Ireland

Use CORU standards, equality and human-rights duties, accessible communication, advocacy and HSE or Tusla complaints routes. Record the person’s wishes, support offered, legal basis, alternatives, proportionality, disagreement and review.

Check whether information sharing is necessary, proportionate and lawful. Explain decisions in a way the person can understand and keep Irish professional and organisational pathways distinct from UK systems.

[CORU codes](https://coru.ie/health-and-social-care-professionals/codes-of-professional-conduct/)

# Quick Reference — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/quick-reference.html

# Quick Reference — Ireland

## Before choosing an action

1. Hear the person and clarify immediate safety.
2. Identify the specific decision, service, setting and jurisdiction.
3. Check authority, consent, reporting duties and privacy.
4. Compare support and less restrictive alternatives.
5. Record evidence, the person’s views, action owners and review.

## Topic routes

- [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): What is the purpose and limit of your role?
- [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?
- [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?
- [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?
- [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?
- [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): How can the person be heard safely and privately?
- [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=children#learningWorkspace): What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?
- [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=ireland&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): What makes participation accessible for this person?

## Before relying on a rule

Check the official source’s current version, commencement and territorial scope. This quick reference cannot determine thresholds or timescales for a live case.

# Practice Scenarios — Ireland — Ireland

Jurisdiction: Ireland
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Ireland practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/ireland/practice-scenarios.html

# Practice Scenarios — Ireland

## Work through a fictional case

Read the scenario, identify the person’s perspective and answer the three questions before revealing the discussion. Compare your reasoning with the worked response and open the suggested modules.

## Check your reasoning

The cases are fictional and the discussions are learning examples. Establish the Ireland source and local route for any legal conclusion. Consider what evidence is missing, alternative explanations, responsibility for next actions and how outcomes will be reviewed.


## Worked cases

### Care and family support

An older adult wants to remain at home after two falls. Their daughter works nights and cannot sustain daily visits.

- Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?
- Which service actually assesses and funds this support?
- What happens if the proposed support is unavailable?

Discussion: Separate the person’s needs from the daughter’s circumstances. Explore available services and practical changes, agree interim safety measures and name who will check whether the plan works. Use the Ireland module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### A decision and a refusal

After a tiring hospital stay, a person refuses a move. Staff interpret the refusal as inability to decide; the person requests an interpreter.

- What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?
- What communication support would help?
- Who has authority for this decision under the applicable law?

Discussion: Arrange language support and suitable timing. Identify the decision and applicable legal criteria. Record the person’s reasoning, check any representative’s authority and distinguish a capacity question from disagreement. Use the Ireland module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Restrictions and objections

A resident lives behind locked doors and is accompanied on outings. The record says they are settled, although they sometimes ask to leave.

- What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?
- What authority is being relied upon?
- How can the person challenge the arrangements?

Discussion: Describe the actual restrictions and hear the person’s account. Examine consent, authority and alternatives through the relevant local legal route. Record objections, independent support and review. Use the Ireland module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Mental-health crisis

A distressed person in an emergency department wants to leave. Compulsory assessment and physical treatment are both proposed.

- What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?
- Who can assess or exercise the relevant power?
- What voluntary or less restrictive support is available?

Discussion: Clarify immediate needs and the purpose of each intervention. Involve authorised professionals through the local pathway, explain rights and identify separate legal bases where needed. Use the Ireland module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Financial control

A relative holds a person’s bank card and answers every question. The person says everything is fine while the relative is present.

- How can the person be heard safely and privately?
- Which reporting pathway applies to this person and setting?
- What immediate action and follow-up are required?

Discussion: Offer safe private communication. Explore coercion, the person’s wishes and immediate safety. Identify reporting requirements and proportionate protective options without assuming a relative has financial authority. Use the Ireland module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Moving into adult services

A 17-year-old with education and daily-living support wants to attend college away from home. Several services expect another team to coordinate the move.

- What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?
- Which reporting duty and receiving agency apply?
- How will education, health and family support coordinate?

Discussion: Ask the young person about goals and support preferences. Map the local education and adult-service processes, confirm age-specific requirements, assign responsibilities and plan continuity rather than relying on a birthday handover. Use the Ireland module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Organisational concerns

Several residents have unexplained injuries. Staff describe rushed care, and earlier concerns have not received a response.

- How can the person be heard safely and privately?
- Which reporting pathway applies to this person and setting?
- What immediate action and follow-up are required?

Discussion: Address immediate safety, preserve relevant evidence and identify the correct safeguarding, regulatory and employer routes. Confirm who will respond and escalate unresolved concerns while protecting residents’ participation. Use the Ireland module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Communication and agreement

A carer reports that meetings are inaccessible and that they felt pressured to agree to a plan. The record states that everyone agreed.

- What makes participation accessible for this person?
- What legal basis permits disclosure of this information?
- How will disagreement and reasons be recorded?

Discussion: Arrange accessible communication and revisit the person’s account. Correct the record through the proper process, explain choices and complaints routes, and review whether the plan is voluntary and workable. Use the Ireland module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

# Terms of Service — Ireland

## Purpose and scope

The Ireland guide is an educational resource for learning and supervision. It does not provide individual legal advice, determine a case outcome or certify professional competence. Use current official sources and the procedures applicable to your role.

## Responsible use

Practice scenarios are fictional. Downloads are learning prompts, not statutory forms. Do not enter identifiable case details into reflections or enquiries. Your browser stores local notes; export your own copy if you need a durable record.

External sources may change. The source library records editorial scope; inclusion of a link or model does not imply endorsement by its publisher. Send corrections with the relevant source and section title through the contact route.

# Learning Map — Aotearoa New Zealand

## A sequence for study

1. [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.
2. [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.
3. [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.
4. [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.
5. [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.
6. [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.
7. [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=children#learningWorkspace): Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.
8. [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

## Put learning into practice

Choose one fictional scenario. Record what is known, the person’s perspective and what still needs checking. Open the source library before answering a legal question. Use supervision to test alternative explanations and a reflection to record the next action.

# Learning Flashcards — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/learning-flashcards.html

# Learning Flashcards — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Recall and explain

The eight decks contain five cards each. Choose a module, answer in your own words, then reveal the answer. Use the linked module and source library for legal detail; a short card cannot reproduce a statutory test.

## Review difficult cards

Explain the distinction with a fictional example. Record uncertainty for supervision and return to the card after reading the source. The cards test learning and do not certify competence.


## Revision cards

### Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand: Where should you begin checking professional foundations in Aotearoa New Zealand?

Start with Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB). Check the professional requirements for your role and the applicable law.

### Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand: How does a formulation differ from a chronology?

It connects evidence, the person’s perspective and possible explanations to a reasoned plan.

### Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand: How can supervision test bias?

Ask what evidence challenges your preferred explanation and whose perspective is missing.

### Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand: What makes a professional record useful?

It distinguishes observations, reported information, analysis, actions and review responsibilities.

### Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand: What makes reflective learning actionable?

A specific change to practice, a way to seek feedback and a date to revisit its impact.

### Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand: Where should you begin checking social care and support in Aotearoa New Zealand?

Open Health of Disabled People Strategy from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand: Can family support be assumed?

No. Explore willingness, ability and sustainability with each person involved.

### Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand: Why distinguish assessment from funding?

A description of need does not itself determine eligibility, availability or costs under a particular programme.

### Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand: What belongs in a support plan?

Desired outcomes, agreed actions, responsible people, contingency and review.

### Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand: What if support is unavailable?

Record the unmet need, interim arrangements and escalation; do not record an unavailable service as an agreed solution.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand: Where should you begin checking decision-making and capacity in Aotearoa New Zealand?

Open SWRB Core Competence Standards from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand: Does a risky refusal alone establish inability to decide?

No. Explore the decision-making process, supports and applicable legal criteria.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand: What support can improve participation?

Accessible information, suitable timing, interpretation and communication aids chosen for the person.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand: Does a family relationship establish decision-making authority?

Do not assume it does. Verify the applicable law and any appointment or authorisation.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand: Why identify the exact decision?

Different decisions can involve different abilities, legal tests and representatives. Avoid a global label.

### Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand: Where should you begin checking restrictions and liberty in Aotearoa New Zealand?

Open Health of Disabled People Strategy from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand: What should a restriction record describe?

Actual arrangements, duration, intensity, effects, ability to leave and the person’s account.

### Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand: Does quiet behaviour demonstrate consent?

Do not assume consent from silence. Explore wishes, understanding, pressure and communication.

### Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand: Can provider policy alone establish legal authority?

A policy must operate within applicable law. Identify the legal basis and scope of the proposed restriction.

### Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand: What should review consider?

Whether the restriction remains justified, less restrictive alternatives, objections and routes to challenge.

### Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand: Where should you begin checking mental health in Aotearoa New Zealand?

Open Ministry of Health mental-health information from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand: Why distinguish admission from treatment?

The legal basis for admission may differ from the authority to provide a particular treatment.

### Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand: What should happen alongside crisis assessment?

Attend to immediate health needs, communication, the person’s account and available support.

### Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand: Can a social worker use every mental-health power?

No. Establish the qualifications, appointment and authority required for the particular role.

### Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand: What does a rights explanation cover?

The proposed action, reasons, available advocacy, review and ways to raise concerns.

### Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand: Where should you begin checking adult safeguarding in Aotearoa New Zealand?

Open Oranga Tamariki practice from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand: Why offer a private conversation?

It may help identify coercion or harm that a person cannot safely describe in front of others.

### Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand: Is proof needed before checking reporting duties?

Do not wait to prove abuse. Consider the applicable reporting threshold and act promptly when it is met.

### Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand: What should a report contain?

Relevant facts, the concern, immediate safety needs, the person’s account and actions already taken.

### Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand: Does a referral complete the response?

No. Confirm receipt, identify responsibility, review safety and escalate unresolved concerns as needed.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: Where should you begin checking children, families and transitions in Aotearoa New Zealand?

Open Whānau searching practice from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: How should the child’s account be recorded?

Use their own words where possible and distinguish what they said from adult interpretation.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: Can one child-protection model settle a legal threshold?

No. A practice model helps enquiry; reporting and intervention require the applicable legal analysis.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: What makes transition planning useful?

Named responsibilities and dates across services, guided by the young person’s goals and continuity of support.

### Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand: Why consider community and cultural relationships?

They may support identity, participation and safety. Ask the family rather than making assumptions.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: Where should you begin checking rights, culture and recording in Aotearoa New Zealand?

Open SWRB Code of Conduct from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: What is data minimisation?

Sharing only the information needed for the identified, lawful purpose.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: What is a culturally responsive first step?

Ask the person how they want to communicate and which cultural or community supports they want involved.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: Why record disagreement?

It preserves the person’s perspective and makes professional reasoning and review more accountable.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand: How do you compare alternatives?

Consider likely benefit, burdens, rights, the person’s preferences and whether a less intrusive option could work.

# Practice Glossary — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/practice-glossary.html

# Practice Glossary — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Use terms in context

Search the glossary, read a definition and open the linked module. These are learning definitions. Statutory terms must be read in their own law and jurisdiction.

## Check understanding

Explain a term in ordinary language and give an example. Distinguish everyday words such as consent, capacity and eligibility from their specific legal meanings. Consult Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB) for professional terminology within its remit.


## Practice glossary

### Professional Foundations

Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.

### Social Care and Support

Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.

### Decision-Making and Capacity

Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.

### Restrictions and Liberty

Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.

### Mental Health

Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.

### Adult Safeguarding

Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.

### Children, Families and Transitions

Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.

### Rights, Culture and Recording

Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

### Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB)

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.

### Advocacy

Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.

### CPD

Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.

### Consent

Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.

### Coercion

Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.

### Eligibility

The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.

### Capacity

Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.

### Representative

Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.

### Proportionality

A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.

### Cultural safety

Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.

### Data minimisation

Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.

### Confidentiality

Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.

### Safeguarding referral

Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.

### Professional supervision

Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.

### Formulation

A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.

### Family network

Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.

### Transition

Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.

### Contingency

An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.

### Review

A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.

### Least restrictive option

An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.

---

# Theory Into Practice — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/theory-into-practice-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Theory Into Practice — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Build a testable explanation

Use the theory finder to generate alternative explanations for a fictional case. Compare what each lens notices about relationships, environment, power, trauma and strengths. Record evidence that would support or challenge your explanation.

## Use models thoughtfully

Theories are shared learning lenses, not country-specific statutory rules. Their inclusion does not imply official adoption in Aotearoa New Zealand. Check suitability, training requirements, cultural context and the person’s account before applying a method.


## Interactive theory lenses

### Ecological Systems Theory

Person, family, housing, community, services, poverty, policy, culture, and environment.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be shaped by pressures around the person, not only by individual behaviour or choice.

- What changed in the environment before the concern escalated?
- Which systems are supporting the person, and which are adding pressure?
- Would risk reduce if housing, income, access, care, or community support changed?

### Strengths-Based Practice

Capabilities, identity, relationships, community, culture, hope, and what is already working.

Hypothesis: The person may have protective strategies or relationships that are hidden by a risk-heavy professional account.

- What has helped the person survive or cope so far?
- Who does the person trust, and what role could they safely play?
- Which strengths are real evidence, and which are optimistic assumptions?

### Trauma-Informed Practice

Safety, trust, choice, collaboration, empowerment, shame, threat responses, and control.

Hypothesis: Behaviour that looks like refusal, avoidance, anger, or disengagement may be a survival response to trauma, coercion, loss, or fear.

- What might feel unsafe or controlling from the person's perspective?
- What helps the person feel more choice and predictability?
- How can we avoid repeating patterns of powerlessness?

### Attachment Theory

Trust, separation, dependency, rejection, fear, care-seeking, and relationship patterns.

Hypothesis: Responses to professionals or carers may reflect previous experiences of care, loss, abandonment, or unsafe relationships.

- How does the person respond when support increases, reduces, or changes?
- Are there patterns of clinging, pushing away, testing, mistrust, or fear?
- What relationship approach is consistent, boundaried, and safe?

### Systems and Family Theory

Roles, rules, communication, repeated patterns, conflict, care dynamics, and network effects.

Hypothesis: The concern may be maintained by relationship patterns, family roles, service responses, or network conflict.

- Who gains or loses if the current pattern changes?
- What role has each person been placed in or taken on?
- How do professional responses affect the family or network pattern?

### Anti-Oppressive and Anti-Discriminatory Practice

Power, oppression, racism, disability, class, gender, sexuality, culture, age, stigma, and access.

Hypothesis: The presenting issue may be intensified by structural inequality, professional power, discrimination, or inaccessible services.

- What barriers has the person faced before we became involved?
- Whose account is being treated as most credible, and why?
- What reasonable adjustments, cultural humility, or advocacy are needed?

### Crisis Theory

Immediate stress, narrowed options, temporary disequilibrium, coping capacity, and stabilisation.

Hypothesis: The person or family may be temporarily overwhelmed and need stabilisation before longer-term planning is realistic.

- What immediate event or loss has exceeded usual coping?
- What needs to happen in the next 24 to 72 hours?
- What can wait until safety, sleep, food, medication, or support is more stable?

### Life Course Theory

Transitions, cumulative disadvantage, ageing, identity, loss, timing, and turning points.

Hypothesis: Current risk or distress may connect to earlier life events, cumulative exclusion, transition, bereavement, or changing identity.

- What transitions or losses are happening now?
- How has cumulative disadvantage shaped options and trust?
- What strengths, relationships, or identities from earlier life still matter?

### Task-Centred Practice

Specific problems, agreed goals, small steps, roles, review, and measurable change.

Hypothesis: The person may benefit from breaking an overwhelming issue into concrete, negotiated tasks with clear review.

- What problem does the person most want to work on first?
- What is the smallest useful next step?
- Who will do what, by when, and how will we know it helped?

---

# Children and Family Practice Models — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/children-and-family-practice-models-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Children and Family Practice Models — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Compare approaches to children and families

Use the model finder to explore enquiry, family relationships, support and safety planning. Begin with the child’s account and daily experience; distinguish observed evidence from adult interpretation.

## Local application

These shared models are educational examples, not a list of officially approved Aotearoa New Zealand programmes. Check training, licensing, local adoption and cultural suitability. A model never replaces the applicable reporting duty or legal threshold.


## Model finder

### Signs of Safety

Child protection mapping, danger statements, safety goals, family network work, scaling, and safety planning.

### Signs of Wellbeing, Success, and Belonging

Family support, children in care, permanency, reunification, stability, identity, and belonging work.

### Family Safeguarding

Whole-family child protection where parental domestic abuse, mental health, substance misuse, trauma, or adult needs affect child safety.

### Contextual Safeguarding

Extra-familial harm, exploitation, peer group risk, school, neighbourhood, online spaces, and adolescent safeguarding.

### Family Group Conferencing

Family-led planning, kinship care, safety planning, pre-proceedings, reunification, and support network building.

### Systemic Practice

Family patterns, repeated cycles, communication, roles, meaning, conflict, and relationship-based formulation.

### Motivational Interviewing

Ambivalence, parental engagement, adolescent risk, substance use, resistance, and behaviour change conversations.

### Solution-Focused Practice

Goal-setting, exceptions, scaling, strengths, future-focused planning, and building on small signs of progress.

### PACE and DDP-Informed Practice

Children affected by trauma, attachment disruption, care experience, shame, mistrust, and blocked trust.

### Safe and Together

Domestic abuse-informed child welfare, perpetrator pattern mapping, protective parent strengths, and child impact.

### Graded Care Profile 2

Neglect assessment, evidence-based care mapping, physical care, safety, love and esteem, and developmental care.

### Restorative Practice

Repair, accountability, family meetings, school relationships, conflict, shame, and shared problem-solving.

# CPD and Reflection Log — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Reflect on learning

Name the activity, date, what you learned and how it could improve practice. Add feedback from supervision or a colleague and choose a next action.

## Keep your record

Reflections save in this browser for Aotearoa New Zealand. Export a text copy or print a PDF; browser clearing and device changes can remove local records. Do not enter identifiable case information. Saving here does not submit evidence to Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB). Check its own requirements separately.

# Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/professional-foundations.html

# Professional Foundations — Aotearoa New Zealand

The Social Workers Registration Board (SWRB) Code of Conduct and ten Core Competence Standards anchor practice. Registered social workers must hold a current practising certificate, follow the Code, undertake CPD and practise within competence. The Code expects respect for Māori as tangata whenua, cultural safety, privacy, accurate records and responsible use of technology.

Use supervision to examine power, culture, language, bias, evidence and the person’s goals. Record what the person and whānau said, what you observed, your analysis, authority and review.

[SWRB Code of Conduct](https://swrb.govt.nz/practice/code-of-conduct/)

---

# Social Care and Support — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/social-care-and-support-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Social care and support — Aotearoa New Zealand

Support may involve health and disability services, Whaikaha, local providers, whānau, iwi and community organisations. Identify the relevant service eligibility, needs assessment, funding and complaints pathway; there is no UK Care Act route.

Begin with the person’s and whānau’s goals, strengths, accessibility and cultural context. Do not assume unpaid whānau support is available or sustainable. Discuss self-determination, options, risks, safeguards and review.

[Health of Disabled People Strategy](https://www.health.govt.nz/strategies-initiatives/health-strategies/health-of-disabled-people-strategy)

---

# Decision-Making and Capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/decision-making-and-capacity-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Decision-making and capacity — Aotearoa New Zealand

Use the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act 1988 and current New Zealand guidance for capacity, welfare guardianship, enduring powers and supported decision-making. Define the decision, support communication and identify the person’s will and preferences. Do not import UK MCA terminology or tests without checking local law.

Consider whānau involvement with the person’s authority, cultural safety, least restrictive options, advocacy, evidence and review. Seek legal or specialist advice where guardianship, compulsory treatment or liberty restrictions arise.

[SWRB Core Competence Standards](https://swrb.govt.nz/practice/core-competence-standards/)

---

# Restrictions and Liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/restrictions-and-liberty-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Restrictions and liberty — Aotearoa New Zealand

There is no single New Zealand DoLS scheme equivalent to England or Wales. Examine the actual restriction, consent, statutory authority, purpose, duration, necessity, proportionality and ability to challenge. Consider the Protection of Personal and Property Rights Act, mental-health law, disability rights and provider policy.

Include the person and whānau, provide accessible information and record less restrictive alternatives. A diagnosis, risk label or provider policy does not itself authorise confinement.

[Health of Disabled People Strategy](https://www.health.govt.nz/strategies-initiatives/health-strategies/health-of-disabled-people-strategy)

---

# Mental Health — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/mental-health-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Mental health — Aotearoa New Zealand

The Mental Health (Compulsory Assessment and Treatment) Act 1992 and current Ministry of Health guidance govern compulsory assessment and treatment. Identify the purpose, responsible clinicians, rights advice, independent advocacy, cultural support and review route. Check current reform information before applying a provision.

Separate compulsory mental-health treatment from capacity, disability support, safeguarding and everyday care. Engage whānau appropriately and respect Māori and Pacific cultural contexts. Record why intervention is necessary and what less restrictive options were considered.

[Ministry of Health mental-health information](https://www.health.govt.nz/health-topics/mental-health)

---

# Adult Safeguarding — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/safeguarding-and-family-violence-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Safeguarding and family violence — Aotearoa New Zealand

Use the relevant health, disability, family-violence and child-protection policy for the service and circumstances. Establish immediate safety, the person’s account, coercion, cultural context, support network, information-sharing basis and desired outcomes.

Where tamariki are involved, contact Oranga Tamariki through the applicable pathway. Adults may need health, disability, police or family-violence responses. Do not invent a UK adult safeguarding threshold; record the New Zealand policy and local escalation route used.

[Oranga Tamariki practice](https://practice.orangatamariki.govt.nz/)

---

# Children, Families and Transitions — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/tamariki-rangatahi-and-wh-nau-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Tamariki, rangatahi and whānau — Aotearoa New Zealand

Oranga Tamariki is the statutory child-care and protection agency. Use the Oranga Tamariki Practice Framework, the Oranga Tamariki Act 1989 and current guidance. Work with tamariki, parents, whānau, hapū and iwi; whānau searching and culturally grounded assessment are core practice considerations.

Listen to the child, explain confidentiality, record facts separately from analysis and coordinate education, health, disability, family support and safety. Consider whakapapa, identity and placement relationships without stereotyping.

[Whānau searching practice](https://practice.orangatamariki.govt.nz/core-practice/working-with-maori/how-to-work-effectively-with-maori/whanau-searching)

# Rights, Culture and Recording — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/rights-culture-and-recording-aotearoa-new-zealand.html

# Rights, culture and recording — Aotearoa New Zealand

Use the SWRB Code, cultural competence, Te Tiriti o Waitangi responsibilities, the New Zealand Disability Strategy and human-rights protections. Ask how the person communicates, what cultural or language support is wanted and who should be involved.

Record the person’s and whānau’s views, authority, evidence, alternatives, proportionality, disagreement and review. Use technology safely and protect privacy.

[SWRB Code of Conduct](https://swrb.govt.nz/practice/code-of-conduct/)

# Quick Reference — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/quick-reference.html

# Quick Reference — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Before choosing an action

1. Hear the person and clarify immediate safety.
2. Identify the specific decision, service, setting and jurisdiction.
3. Check authority, consent, reporting duties and privacy.
4. Compare support and less restrictive alternatives.
5. Record evidence, the person’s views, action owners and review.

## Topic routes

- [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): What is the purpose and limit of your role?
- [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?
- [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?
- [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?
- [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?
- [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): How can the person be heard safely and privately?
- [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=children#learningWorkspace): What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?
- [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=new-zealand&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): What makes participation accessible for this person?

## Before relying on a rule

Check the official source’s current version, commencement and territorial scope. This quick reference cannot determine thresholds or timescales for a live case.

# Practice Scenarios — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/practice-scenarios.html

# Practice Scenarios — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Work through a fictional case

Read the scenario, identify the person’s perspective and answer the three questions before revealing the discussion. Compare your reasoning with the worked response and open the suggested modules.

## Check your reasoning

The cases are fictional and the discussions are learning examples. Establish the Aotearoa New Zealand source and local route for any legal conclusion. Consider what evidence is missing, alternative explanations, responsibility for next actions and how outcomes will be reviewed.


## Worked cases

### Care and family support

An older adult wants to remain at home after two falls. Their daughter works nights and cannot sustain daily visits.

- Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers?
- Which service actually assesses and funds this support?
- What happens if the proposed support is unavailable?

Discussion: Separate the person’s needs from the daughter’s circumstances. Explore available services and practical changes, agree interim safety measures and name who will check whether the plan works. Use the Aotearoa New Zealand module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### A decision and a refusal

After a tiring hospital stay, a person refuses a move. Staff interpret the refusal as inability to decide; the person requests an interpreter.

- What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned?
- What communication support would help?
- Who has authority for this decision under the applicable law?

Discussion: Arrange language support and suitable timing. Identify the decision and applicable legal criteria. Record the person’s reasoning, check any representative’s authority and distinguish a capacity question from disagreement. Use the Aotearoa New Zealand module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Restrictions and objections

A resident lives behind locked doors and is accompanied on outings. The record says they are settled, although they sometimes ask to leave.

- What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person?
- What authority is being relied upon?
- How can the person challenge the arrangements?

Discussion: Describe the actual restrictions and hear the person’s account. Examine consent, authority and alternatives through the relevant local legal route. Record objections, independent support and review. Use the Aotearoa New Zealand module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Mental-health crisis

A distressed person in an emergency department wants to leave. Compulsory assessment and physical treatment are both proposed.

- What is the purpose of each proposed intervention?
- Who can assess or exercise the relevant power?
- What voluntary or less restrictive support is available?

Discussion: Clarify immediate needs and the purpose of each intervention. Involve authorised professionals through the local pathway, explain rights and identify separate legal bases where needed. Use the Aotearoa New Zealand module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Financial control

A relative holds a person’s bank card and answers every question. The person says everything is fine while the relative is present.

- How can the person be heard safely and privately?
- Which reporting pathway applies to this person and setting?
- What immediate action and follow-up are required?

Discussion: Offer safe private communication. Explore coercion, the person’s wishes and immediate safety. Identify reporting requirements and proportionate protective options without assuming a relative has financial authority. Use the Aotearoa New Zealand module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Moving into adult services

A 17-year-old with education and daily-living support wants to attend college away from home. Several services expect another team to coordinate the move.

- What does the child say or show about safety and daily life?
- Which reporting duty and receiving agency apply?
- How will education, health and family support coordinate?

Discussion: Ask the young person about goals and support preferences. Map the local education and adult-service processes, confirm age-specific requirements, assign responsibilities and plan continuity rather than relying on a birthday handover. Use the Aotearoa New Zealand module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Organisational concerns

Several residents have unexplained injuries. Staff describe rushed care, and earlier concerns have not received a response.

- How can the person be heard safely and privately?
- Which reporting pathway applies to this person and setting?
- What immediate action and follow-up are required?

Discussion: Address immediate safety, preserve relevant evidence and identify the correct safeguarding, regulatory and employer routes. Confirm who will respond and escalate unresolved concerns while protecting residents’ participation. Use the Aotearoa New Zealand module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

### Communication and agreement

A carer reports that meetings are inaccessible and that they felt pressured to agree to a plan. The record states that everyone agreed.

- What makes participation accessible for this person?
- What legal basis permits disclosure of this information?
- How will disagreement and reasons be recorded?

Discussion: Arrange accessible communication and revisit the person’s account. Correct the record through the proper process, explain choices and complaints routes, and review whether the plan is voluntary and workable. Use the Aotearoa New Zealand module and source library to identify the applicable framework.

## How to verify a rule

Open the official source, check its publisher, current version, territorial scope and commencement, then identify the relevant provision and local service procedure. Record the exact link and date accessed. A portal link is a starting point, not evidence that every provision has been checked.

## Editorial status

Final learning-guide release, 8 September 2026. Professional-body references were checked during the editorial review. Independent practitioner review has not been recorded. Software checks verify rendering and references, not the correctness of every legal interpretation.

# About Us — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/about-us.html

# About Us — Aotearoa New Zealand

## About this resource

Daily Mindset Moments CIC, founded by Raymond Hill, provides this structured social-work learning resource. It supports students, practitioners and supervisors with modules, fictional exercises, source links and private reflections.

## Aotearoa New Zealand context

This guide separates the learning material for Aotearoa New Zealand from the other practice locations. Shared theories support enquiry; laws, professional requirements and service pathways must be checked locally. Read the source library for scope and editorial status.

# Contact Us — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Feedback and corrections

Contact [Daily Mindset Moments CIC](mailto:info@daily-mindset-moments.com) with the selected location, section title, source URL and a description of the correction. The contact form below is for website enquiries.

## Keep enquiries appropriate

Do not include identifiable case information. This website is not an emergency or casework reporting service. Use the responsible local agency, employer and emergency services for urgent or live practice concerns.

# Privacy Policy — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/privacy-policy.html

# Privacy Policy — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Learning stored on your device

The app stores your selected location, reading progress, confidence, saved reflections and unfinished reflection fields in this browser. Records are separated by location. They are not submitted to a professional body. Export or print a copy before clearing browser data or changing devices.

## Website enquiries

If you use the contact form, the details you submit are sent to the website’s form service and operator. Do not send confidential case information. External source websites have their own privacy policies.

## Your records

Use Delete reflection to remove saved entries. Clearing this site’s browser storage removes local progress and notes. Contact [Daily Mindset Moments CIC](mailto:info@daily-mindset-moments.com) about information sent through an enquiry.

# Terms of Service — Aotearoa New Zealand — Aotearoa New Zealand

Jurisdiction: Aotearoa New Zealand
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent Aotearoa New Zealand practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/new-zealand/terms-of-service.html

# Terms of Service — Aotearoa New Zealand

## Purpose and scope

The Aotearoa New Zealand guide is an educational resource for learning and supervision. It does not provide individual legal advice, determine a case outcome or certify professional competence. Use current official sources and the procedures applicable to your role.

## Responsible use

Practice scenarios are fictional. Downloads are learning prompts, not statutory forms. Do not enter identifiable case details into reflections or enquiries. Your browser stores local notes; export your own copy if you need a durable record.

## Sources and corrections

External sources may change. The source library records editorial scope; inclusion of a link or model does not imply endorsement by its publisher. Send corrections with the relevant source and section title through the contact route.

# Start Here — New South Wales

## Your New South Wales learning guide

## Start learning

Read [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace), choose a topic from [Learning Map](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=map#learningWorkspace), then practise with [Practice Scenarios](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=scenarios#learningWorkspace). ## Scope

Eight modules, forty flashcards, a glossary, eight fictional scenarios and ten recording prompts support revision and supervision. This is a final learning-guide release. It is not an exhaustive account of law, a statutory form or a regulator-approved training programme. The source library explains how to check the applicable version and local route.

# Learning Map — New South Wales — New South Wales

Jurisdiction: New South Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent New South Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-nsw/learning-map.html

# Learning Map — New South Wales

## A sequence for study

1. [Professional Foundations](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=foundations#learningWorkspace): Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.
2. [Social Care and Support](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=care-support#learningWorkspace): Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.
3. [Decision-Making and Capacity](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=mca#learningWorkspace): Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.
4. [Restrictions and Liberty](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=dols#learningWorkspace): Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.
5. [Mental Health](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=mha#learningWorkspace): Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.
6. [Adult Safeguarding](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=safeguarding#learningWorkspace): Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.
7. [Children, Families and Transitions](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=children#learningWorkspace): Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.
8. [Rights, Culture and Recording](/?jurisdiction=australia-nsw&resource=rights#learningWorkspace): Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

## Put learning into practice

Choose one fictional scenario. Record what is known, the person’s perspective and what still needs checking. Open the source library before answering a legal question. Use supervision to test alternative explanations and a reflection to record the next action.

# Learning Flashcards — New South Wales — New South Wales

Jurisdiction: New South Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent New South Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-nsw/learning-flashcards.html

# Learning Flashcards — New South Wales

## Recall and explain

The eight decks contain five cards each. Choose a module, answer in your own words, then reveal the answer. Use the linked module and source library for legal detail; a short card cannot reproduce a statutory test.

## Review difficult cards

Explain the distinction with a fictional example. Record uncertainty for supervision and return to the card after reading the source. The cards test learning and do not certify competence.


## Revision cards

### Professional Foundations — New South Wales: Where should you begin checking professional foundations in New South Wales?

Start with Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW). Check the professional requirements for your role and the applicable law.

### Professional Foundations — New South Wales: How does a formulation differ from a chronology?

It connects evidence, the person’s perspective and possible explanations to a reasoned plan.

### Professional Foundations — New South Wales: How can supervision test bias?

Ask what evidence challenges your preferred explanation and whose perspective is missing.

### Professional Foundations — New South Wales: What makes a professional record useful?

It distinguishes observations, reported information, analysis, actions and review responsibilities.

### Professional Foundations — New South Wales: What makes reflective learning actionable?

A specific change to practice, a way to seek feedback and a date to revisit its impact.

### Social Care and Support — New South Wales: Where should you begin checking social care and support in New South Wales?

Open NDIS and service access from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Social Care and Support — New South Wales: Can family support be assumed?

No. Explore willingness, ability and sustainability with each person involved.

### Social Care and Support — New South Wales: Why distinguish assessment from funding?

A description of need does not itself determine eligibility, availability or costs under a particular programme.

### Social Care and Support — New South Wales: What belongs in a support plan?

Desired outcomes, agreed actions, responsible people, contingency and review.

### Social Care and Support — New South Wales: What if support is unavailable?

Record the unmet need, interim arrangements and escalation; do not record an unavailable service as an agreed solution.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — New South Wales: Where should you begin checking decision-making and capacity in New South Wales?

Open NCAT consent and guardianship from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — New South Wales: Does a risky refusal alone establish inability to decide?

No. Explore the decision-making process, supports and applicable legal criteria.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — New South Wales: What support can improve participation?

Accessible information, suitable timing, interpretation and communication aids chosen for the person.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — New South Wales: Does a family relationship establish decision-making authority?

Do not assume it does. Verify the applicable law and any appointment or authorisation.

### Decision-Making and Capacity — New South Wales: Why identify the exact decision?

Different decisions can involve different abilities, legal tests and representatives. Avoid a global label.

### Restrictions and Liberty — New South Wales: Where should you begin checking restrictions and liberty in New South Wales?

Open NCAT consent and guardianship and NSW mental-health legislation from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Restrictions and Liberty — New South Wales: What should a restriction record describe?

Actual arrangements, duration, intensity, effects, ability to leave and the person’s account.

### Restrictions and Liberty — New South Wales: Does quiet behaviour demonstrate consent?

Do not assume consent from silence. Explore wishes, understanding, pressure and communication.

### Restrictions and Liberty — New South Wales: Can provider policy alone establish legal authority?

A policy must operate within applicable law. Identify the legal basis and scope of the proposed restriction.

### Restrictions and Liberty — New South Wales: What should review consider?

Whether the restriction remains justified, less restrictive alternatives, objections and routes to challenge.

### Mental Health — New South Wales: Where should you begin checking mental health in New South Wales?

Open NSW mental-health legislation from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Mental Health — New South Wales: Why distinguish admission from treatment?

The legal basis for admission may differ from the authority to provide a particular treatment.

### Mental Health — New South Wales: What should happen alongside crisis assessment?

Attend to immediate health needs, communication, the person’s account and available support.

### Mental Health — New South Wales: Can a social worker use every mental-health power?

No. Establish the qualifications, appointment and authority required for the particular role.

### Mental Health — New South Wales: What does a rights explanation cover?

The proposed action, reasons, available advocacy, review and ways to raise concerns.

### Adult Safeguarding — New South Wales: Where should you begin checking adult safeguarding in New South Wales?

Open NSW adult safeguarding from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Adult Safeguarding — New South Wales: Why offer a private conversation?

It may help identify coercion or harm that a person cannot safely describe in front of others.

### Adult Safeguarding — New South Wales: Is proof needed before checking reporting duties?

Do not wait to prove abuse. Consider the applicable reporting threshold and act promptly when it is met.

### Adult Safeguarding — New South Wales: What should a report contain?

Relevant facts, the concern, immediate safety needs, the person’s account and actions already taken.

### Adult Safeguarding — New South Wales: Does a referral complete the response?

No. Confirm receipt, identify responsibility, review safety and escalate unresolved concerns as needed.

### Children, Families and Transitions — New South Wales: Where should you begin checking children, families and transitions in New South Wales?

Open DCJ child protection and mandatory reporting from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Children, Families and Transitions — New South Wales: How should the child’s account be recorded?

Use their own words where possible and distinguish what they said from adult interpretation.

### Children, Families and Transitions — New South Wales: Can one child-protection model settle a legal threshold?

No. A practice model helps enquiry; reporting and intervention require the applicable legal analysis.

### Children, Families and Transitions — New South Wales: What makes transition planning useful?

Named responsibilities and dates across services, guided by the young person’s goals and continuity of support.

### Children, Families and Transitions — New South Wales: Why consider community and cultural relationships?

They may support identity, participation and safety. Ask the family rather than making assumptions.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — New South Wales: Where should you begin checking rights, culture and recording in New South Wales?

Open NSW legislation register from the module. Confirm scope, version and local procedures.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — New South Wales: What is data minimisation?

Sharing only the information needed for the identified, lawful purpose.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — New South Wales: What is a culturally responsive first step?

Ask the person how they want to communicate and which cultural or community supports they want involved.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — New South Wales: Why record disagreement?

It preserves the person’s perspective and makes professional reasoning and review more accountable.

### Rights, Culture and Recording — New South Wales: How do you compare alternatives?

Consider likely benefit, burdens, rights, the person’s preferences and whether a less intrusive option could work.

# Student and Newly Qualified Pathway — New South Wales

## Plan your learning

Work through the eight activities with a practice educator or supervisor. Use fictional examples, identify sources and explain your reasoning before looking at the worked scenario.

## Evidence of development

For each activity record one learning point, feedback received and a change to try. These exercises do not replace local qualification, placement, registration or continuing-development requirements. Consult Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) and your education provider for those requirements.


## Pathway activities

### Professional Foundations

Using a fictional New South Wales case: What is the purpose and limit of your role? Which professional standard informs the next action? How will supervision test your reasoning?

### Social Care and Support

Using a fictional New South Wales case: Which needs and outcomes belong to the person and to carers? Which service actually assesses and funds this support? What happens if the proposed support is unavailable?

### Decision-Making and Capacity

Using a fictional New South Wales case: What is the precise decision and why is ability to decide questioned? What communication support would help? Who has authority for this decision under the applicable law?

### Restrictions and Liberty

Using a fictional New South Wales case: What restrictions actually operate and how do they affect the person? What authority is being relied upon? How can the person challenge the arrangements?

### Mental Health

Using a fictional New South Wales case: What is the purpose of each proposed intervention? Who can assess or exercise the relevant power? What voluntary or less restrictive support is available?

### Adult Safeguarding

Using a fictional New South Wales case: How can the person be heard safely and privately? Which reporting pathway applies to this person and setting? What immediate action and follow-up are required?

### Children, Families and Transitions

Using a fictional New South Wales case: What does the child say or show about safety and daily life? Which reporting duty and receiving agency apply? How will education, health and family support coordinate?

### Rights, Culture and Recording

Using a fictional New South Wales case: What makes participation accessible for this person? What legal basis permits disclosure of this information? How will disagreement and reasons be recorded?

# Practice Glossary — New South Wales — New South Wales

Jurisdiction: New South Wales
Final learning guide. See the Source Library for references and review scope. Independent New South Wales practitioner review is not recorded.
Source: https://social-work-resource.netlify.app/learning/australia-nsw/practice-glossary.html

# Practice Glossary — New South Wales

## Use terms in context

Search the glossary, read a definition and open the linked module. These are learning definitions. Statutory terms must be read in their own law and jurisdiction.

## Check understanding

Explain a term in ordinary language and give an example. Distinguish everyday words such as consent, capacity and eligibility from their specific legal meanings. Consult Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW) for professional terminology within its remit.


## Practice glossary

### Professional Foundations

Professional role, ethics, competence, supervision and accountable decisions.

### Social Care and Support

Needs, strengths, access to support, family responsibilities and service planning.

### Decision-Making and Capacity

Decision support, consent and the authority for someone else to decide.

### Restrictions and Liberty

Restrictions, legal authority, less restrictive options and review.

### Mental Health

Mental-health support, crisis response, treatment and rights.

### Adult Safeguarding

Abuse, neglect, coercion, safe enquiry and the appropriate protective response.

### Children, Families and Transitions

Child participation, family support, child protection and transitions.

### Rights, Culture and Recording

Participation, privacy, cultural safety and clear recording.

### Australian Association of Social Workers (AASW)

The professional body identified for this guide. Check its remit and the requirements that apply to your role.

### Advocacy

Support to express views, understand choices and participate; statutory entitlements depend on the local framework.

### CPD

Continuing professional development: learning, reflection and evidence of improvement.

### Consent

Agreement to a specific action; check the applicable requirements for information, voluntariness and ability to consent.

### Coercion

Pressure or control that can affect expressed wishes and freedom to act.

### Eligibility

The criteria for a particular service or programme; distinct from a description of need.

### Capacity

Ability to make the relevant decision under the applicable legal framework; avoid a global label.

### Representative

Someone with a defined support or decision-making role; verify the source and scope of authority.

### Proportionality

A reasoned comparison of intended benefit, burdens, rights and alternatives.

### Cultural safety

Attention to power, identity and the person’s experience of a service, informed by their preferences.

### Data minimisation

Using or sharing only information needed for an identified lawful purpose.

### Confidentiality

Protecting information while understanding and explaining lawful exceptions.

### Safeguarding referral

Communicating a concern to the appropriate agency; confirm the applicable route and follow-up.

### Professional supervision

Structured discussion of decisions, ethics, skills, wellbeing and accountability.

### Formulation

A reasoned account connecting evidence and possible explanations to a plan.

### Family network

Relationships that may offer support; availability, safety and willingness need assessment.

### Transition

Planned change between services or life stages, with continuity and named responsibilities.

### Contingency

An agreed response if risks increase or the preferred plan cannot operate.

### Review

A planned check of outcomes, changing circumstances and whether actions remain appropriate.

### Least restrictive option

An option that can achieve the purpose with less interference in rights and freedom.
